concepts.name: Galerkin Method
concepts.explanation: The Galerkin method is a foundational approach in the Finite Element Method (FEM) for solving differential equations. It involves approximating the solution of a problem by projecting it onto a finite-dimensional space of basis functions. This method ensures that the residual of the differential equation is orthogonal to the chosen basis functions, leading to a system of algebraic equations. Boris Galerkin introduced this technique, which forms the theoretical basis for modern FEM formulations.
concepts.mathematical_formulation: \int_{\Omega} w(x) \left( \frac{d^2 u}{dx^2} + f(x) \right) dx = 0, \quad \text{for all } w(x) \in V

concepts.name: Curved Elements
concepts.explanation: Curved elements are specialized finite elements used to better approximate complex geometries in FEM. They allow for more accurate modeling of domains with curved boundaries by using higher-order polynomial shapes. This approach reduces discretization errors compared to straight-edged elements. The use of curved elements is particularly critical in weak Galerkin methods, where they enhance the flexibility of the solution space.
concepts.mathematical_formulation: x(\xi, \eta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} N_i(\xi, \eta) X_i, \quad \text{where } X_i \text{ are control points}

concepts.name: Limit Analysis
concepts.explanation: Finite Element Limit Analysis (FELA) is a technique to compute the upper or lower bound plastic collapse load of a mechanical system. It uses optimization algorithms instead of time-stepping, making it efficient for geotechnical problems. FELA is applicable to both kinematic and equilibrium formulations, depending on the problem's constraints. This method is widely used in soil mechanics for stability analysis.

concepts.name: Spectral Element Method (SEM)
concepts.explanation: SEM is a FEM variant using high-degree piecewise polynomials as basis functions, achieving high-order accuracy. It leverages orthogonal polynomials like Chebyshev or Lagrange polynomials over non-uniform nodes, enabling exponential error reduction with increasing polynomial order. SEM places nodal points at Legendre-Gauss-Lobatto (LGL) points, facilitating mass lumping and collocation procedures. This method excels in computational fluid dynamics and seismic wave modeling but struggles with complex geometries compared to traditional FEM.
concepts.mathematical_formulation: u_N \in V_N: a(u_N, v_N) = \langle f, v_N \rangle \quad \forall v_N \in V_N

concepts.name: Additive Schwarz Method
concepts.explanation: A domain decomposition technique for solving PDEs by dividing the computational domain into subdomains. It combines solutions from overlapping subdomains using weighted sums, improving convergence for elliptic problems. The method's nonuniform weighting, based on smoothed sign functions, enhances performance for spectral element solvers. It is particularly effective for Poisson equations and can be integrated with multigrid strategies for faster convergence.

concepts.name: Mass Lumping
concepts.explanation: A technique to simplify the mass matrix in FEM by approximating it as diagonal, reducing computational costs. In SEM, this is achieved by placing nodes at LGL points and using Gauss-Lobatto quadrature. Mass lumping enables efficient time integration with methods like the central difference method (CDM). It is critical for real-time simulations but may sacrifice some accuracy compared to consistent mass matrices.

procedures.title: Discretization of the Domain
procedures.description: The physical domain is divided into smaller, simpler subdomains called elements. This process, known as meshing, allows the problem to be approximated using piecewise functions. The choice of element type (e.g., triangular, quadrilateral) depends on the geometry and required accuracy. Curved elements may be used for complex boundaries to improve approximation.

procedures.title: Formulation of Weak Form
procedures.description: The strong form of the governing differential equation is converted into a weak form by multiplying with a test function and integrating over the domain. This step ensures that the solution satisfies the equation in an integral sense, reducing the smoothness requirements for the approximate solution. The Galerkin method is often used to select the test functions as the same as the basis functions.

procedures.title: Assembly and Solution
procedures.description: The local element equations are assembled into a global system of algebraic equations. This involves summing contributions from all elements and applying boundary conditions. The resulting system is solved using numerical methods such as direct solvers or iterative techniques. For limit analysis, optimization algorithms replace traditional solvers to compute collapse loads directly.

procedures.title: Discretization of Domain
procedures.description: Divide the computational domain into non-overlapping elements. For SEM, elements are defined with high-degree polynomial basis functions. Nodes are placed at LGL points to enable mass lumping. This step ensures the geometry is approximated while maintaining flexibility for complex shapes. The choice of polynomial order directly impacts accuracy and computational cost.

procedures.title: Weak Formulation and Assembly
procedures.description: Convert the PDE into a weak form using test functions. Apply the Galerkin method by projecting the solution onto a finite-dimensional space. Integrate the weak form over elements, using Gauss-Lobatto quadrature for efficiency. Assemble local stiffness and mass matrices into global system matrices. This step ensures the problem is mathematically well-posed and numerically stable.

procedures.title: Solution of Linear System
procedures.description: Solve the resulting linear system using iterative or direct solvers. For large-scale problems, preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) methods are preferred. Multigrid techniques, like V-cycles with Schwarz smoothers, accelerate convergence. The choice of solver depends on problem size, sparsity, and desired accuracy. Iterative methods are favored for their memory efficiency.

equations.name: Galerkin Weak Form
equations.latex: \int_{\Omega} w(x) \left( \frac{d^2 u}{dx^2} + f(x) \right) dx = 0, \quad \text{for all } w(x) \in V
equations.explanation: a(u, v) represents the bilinear form capturing the PDE's differential operator, f is the source term, and v is a test function. This equation ensures the solution satisfies the PDE in an integral sense, reducing regularity requirements. The space V is a finite-dimensional subspace of the Sobolev space H^1(Ω).

equations.name: Curved Element Mapping
equations.explanation: This equation maps local coordinates $ (\xi, \eta) $ to global coordinates $ x $ using shape functions $ N_i $ and control points $ X_i $. It enables curved elements to model complex geometries accurately.

equations.name: Limit Analysis Optimization
equations.explanation: This optimization problem computes the collapse load by minimizing the work done by stresses $ \mathbf{\sigma} $ under yield conditions $ K $. $ \mathbf{\varepsilon} $ represents the strain tensor, and the integral is over the domain $ \Omega $.

equations.name: Residual Reduction Formula
equations.explanation: This bounds the residual reduction per iteration, where C and γ are constants, N is the degrees of freedom. It quantifies the exponential convergence of SEM with increasing polynomial order. The formula highlights the efficiency of high-order methods in reducing errors rapidly.

equations.name: Mass Lumping Approximation
equations.explanation: M_{ij} is the mass matrix entry, δ_{ij} is the Kronecker delta, w_q are quadrature weights, and x_q are LGL nodes. This approximation diagonalizes the mass matrix, enabling explicit time integration. It relies on the orthogonality of basis functions at quadrature points.

rules.explanation: The mesh must be sufficiently refined to ensure numerical results converge to the true solution. Coarse meshes may lead to inaccurate predictions, especially near stress concentrations or curved boundaries. Adaptive meshing techniques are often used to refine regions of interest.

The choice of element type (e.g., linear, quadratic, curved) depends on the problem's geometry and required accuracy. Curved elements improve accuracy for complex domains, while higher-order elements reduce discretization errors in smooth solutions.

Boundary conditions must be correctly applied to ensure the problem's physical constraints are satisfied. Incorrect implementation can lead to non-physical solutions or solver failures. Essential and natural boundary conditions are treated differently in the weak form.

Use high-degree polynomials (e.g., SEM) to achieve exponential error decay. This reduces the number of degrees of freedom compared to low-order FEM, especially for smooth solutions. High-order methods are critical for high-frequency wave simulations but require careful meshing.

Place nodes at LGL points to enable mass lumping and collocation. This reduces computational costs and improves time integration stability. Nonuniform spacing also enhances accuracy for problems with localized features.

Apply Schwarz methods to decompose problems into subdomains, enabling parallel computation. Nonuniform weighting improves convergence for heterogeneous problems. This is essential for large-scale simulations beyond single-processor capabilities.
